description: Ekibimiz yazılım, veri analizi ve tasarım yetkinliklerine sahip. NASA'nın açık verilerini kullanarak yaratıcı ve uygulanabilir çözümler geliştirmeye odaklanıyoruz. Bizimle birlikte heyecanla çalışacak, vizyoner ve enerjik yeni takım arkadaşları arıyoruz. Özellikle Python/veri analitiği, frontend geliştirme veya UI/UX tasarımı/3D modelleme alanlarında beceri sahibiyseniz bize katılın. Gelin, Sivas’tan uzaya uzanan bu 48 saatlik macerayı birlikte yazalım!
summary:
Mucilage Detective is an interactive web application that uses 22 years of NASA Earth observation data (2003–2024) to detect long-term trends in the conditions behind marine mucilage (“sea snot”) outbreaks in Türkiye’s seas, with a focus on the Sea of Marmara. We combined MODIS-Aqua sea surface temperature, chlorophyll-a and fluorescence data with MERRA-2 surface wind from NASA Giovanni. We tested each series for trends using the Mann-Kendall test with Hamed-Rao correction and measured their size with Sen’s slope.

The results show that all three seas are warming significantly, with the Marmara warming fastest at +0.83 °C per decade, while wind shows no trend. Before the 2020–21 and 2024 outbreaks, the Marmara was 1.4–1.6 °C warmer than normal.

The app turns these findings into a risk atlas of 16 coastal sites with “what-if” scenarios, statistical trend analysis and machine learning models that predict chlorophyll from climate data. Mucilage devastated fisheries, tourism and seafloor life in 2021. Our tool helps agencies, fishers and researchers track when conditions are becoming favourable for mucilage.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mucilage Detective is an interactive web application that asks one question: are the conditions behind marine mucilage (“sea snot”) outbreaks becoming more common in Türkiye’s seas? It focuses on the Sea of Marmara, which suffered major outbreaks in 2007–08, 2020–21 (the largest on record) and 2024. The Aegean and Black Seas are analysed the same way for comparison.

We downloaded 22 years (2003–2024, 264 months, no gaps) of monthly area-averaged NASA data from Giovanni:

  • MODIS-Aqua: sea surface temperature and chlorophyll-a.
  • MERRA-2: surface wind.
  • MODIS fluorescence line height (FLH): an independent check of chlorophyll in the turbid Marmara waters.

The Python back end removes the seasonal cycle by subtracting each month’s long-term mean. It then tests each series for trends with the Mann-Kendall test with Hamed-Rao correction for autocorrelation, and measures their size with Sen’s slope.

The app has five pages:

  • Explore: 22-year trends for each sea on a 3D globe, how mucilage forms, and a sourced chronology of outbreaks.
  • Simulation: a risk atlas of 16 coastal sites on an interactive map. You can play 2003–2024 month by month, compare any month with a chosen historical baseline, and run “what-if” scenarios with sliders for temperature, wind and chlorophyll. The risk index combines warm water (35%), calm wind (25%) and phytoplankton (40%) through logistic curves, weighted by each site’s sensitivity.
  • Statistics: trend tests, Sen’s slope and deseasonalised anomaly charts, with outbreak periods marked.
  • Model: Random Forest, XGBoost and SVR models that predict chlorophyll-a from climate inputs. They are trained on 2003–2019 and tested blind on 2020–2024, including the 2021 outbreak.
  • Sources & Data: the full data catalogue and peer-reviewed literature.

Key findings:

  • All three seas are warming significantly (p < 0.001). The Marmara warms fastest at +0.83 °C per decade.
  • Wind shows no trend.
  • Before the 2020–21 and 2024 outbreaks, the Marmara was 1.4–1.6 °C warmer than normal.
  • The best model (Random Forest) explains about 32% of month-to-month chlorophyll variation in unseen years. Sea temperature is its most important input.
Benefits and intended impact

Mucilage devastated fisheries, tourism and seafloor life in 2021. Our tool turns satellite data into something non-specialists can use:

  • Municipalities and environmental agencies can see when conditions are becoming favourable for mucilage.
  • Fishers and aquaculture farms can understand the risk at their coast.
  • Teachers and students can explore real climate trends.

Our long-term goal is a near-real-time early warning system for the Sea of Marmara and the wider Mediterranean.

Tools, languages, hardware and software
  • Data: NASA Giovanni (MODIS-Aqua L3 4 km; MERRA-2 0.5° × 0.625°).
  • Back end (Python 3.12): pandas and NumPy for data processing, pymannkendall for trend tests, scikit-learn and XGBoost for machine learning, FastAPI and Uvicorn for the API.
  • Front end (JavaScript): React and Vite, with Leaflet for the map (OpenStreetMap, CARTO and Esri basemaps), Plotly for charts, and d3-geo with Natural Earth data for the 3D globe.
  • Development: VS Code, Git and GitHub; deployed on Vercel. We worked on standard laptops running Windows; no special hardware was needed.
  • AI assistance: we used an AI assistant (Claude) for coding support, debugging and checking sources. All data, results and claims were verified by the team.
Creativity

Instead of only showing that the sea is warming, we connected long-term NASA trends to a real ecological problem and made them explorable:

  • Seeing trends over time: a time player that “replays” 22 years of conditions.
  • Testing scenarios: “what-if” sliders that show how each coastal site would respond to warmer water or weaker wind.
  • Explaining the process: a visual explanation of how mucilage forms, marking which factors satellites can measure and which they cannot.
  • Being open about limits: we cross-check chlorophyll with a second satellite product (FLH) and test our models blind on the years of the largest outbreak.
Factors the team considered
  • Scientific validity: we used tests that suit climate data (non-parametric, corrected for autocorrelation), split the model data by date to avoid leakage, and linked every historical claim to a peer-reviewed source.
  • Honesty about limits: the risk score shows favourable conditions; it is not a forecast. Satellites see only the surface and cannot measure nutrients or stratification, which are key mucilage drivers. Our models predict chlorophyll, not mucilage itself.
  • Accessibility: clear explanations on every page, colour legends, and simple language for non-experts.
  • Reproducibility: open code, a data catalogue with Giovanni links, and step-by-step run instructions in the README.
